summary: This unit teaches brazing and silver soldering: joining metals with a filler that melts above 450 °C but below the metals being joined, drawn into a close-fitting joint by capillary action. You will learn to choose fillers, fluxes and heating methods, design and prepare joints, braze and braze weld safely with gas equipment, inspect and test the joints, find the causes of faults, and plan, cost, lead and report on brazing work.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **brazing**, **silver soldering** (the trade name for brazing with silver alloys) and **braze welding**. These processes join copper, brass, steel, stainless steel and cast iron, and join unlike metals to each other, at a much lower temperature than welding, because the parent metals are **never melted**.

You will meet brazing on air-conditioning and refrigeration pipework, copper plumbing and solar water heaters, brass fittings, carbide-tipped tools, bicycle and furniture frames, and repairs to cast iron and brass. At Level 3 you also plan the job, write and prove a brazing procedure, inspect and test the joints, lead the team and report on faults and failures.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and fabricators, plumbers and refrigeration and air-conditioning workers who braze. You should already be able to set up and use an oxy-acetylene or air-propane set safely.

What this means in the workshop
rows: Tell brazing from soldering and welding, and explain capillary action, wetting, flux and melting range.
Control fume (especially cadmium and zinc), fire, gas, pressure and flux hazards for yourself and your team.
Use gas equipment and choose a heating method
Set up, test, light, adjust and shut down oxy-fuel and air-fuel sets; choose torch, induction or furnace heating.
Choose the filler and flux for the metals, the joint and the service, and store them correctly.
Set the joint type, overlap and clearance, allow for expansion, and clean, fit and support the parts.
Heat evenly, feed the filler at the right moment, control the heat, and clean the joint afterwards.
Inspect by eye, peel and section sample joints, and pressure or leak test assemblies.
Name the faults, their causes and what to change in the procedure.
Write and prove a procedure, work out materials, cost and time, coach the team and write reports.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning and procedures, safety, gas equipment, fillers, fluxes, joint design, cleaning, heating, inspection, faults, supervision and reporting.

A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as preform, pickle, fillet, firebrick, burr, dye penetrant, nitrogen, and small calculations) and longer answers that explain a plan, a choice of materials, a safe system, a test or a fault.

**Practical tasks**: planning, silver brazing and water pressure testing a copper manifold to a written procedure, and brazing dissimilar-metal lap joints with peel and section tests and a written report.

blocks.note: Many marks depend on reasons: why this filler, why this gap, why this heating method. When you learn a fact, learn the reason with it.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Process
Filler melts at
Parent metal
How the joint is made
rows: Capillary flow into a close joint; low strength
Above 450 °C, but below the parent metals (silver alloys about 600–800 °C)
Capillary flow into a close joint; strong
Filler laid in a groove or as a fillet, like a weld, **without** capillary flow
At or above the parent metal

blocks.note: 'Silver solder' on a packet can mean a silver **brazing** alloy (melting at 600 °C or more) or a tin-silver **soft** solder (about 220 °C). Read the melting range on the packet before you use it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When two clean surfaces are held very close together, a liquid is drawn into the gap between them, even upwards against gravity. This is **capillary action**: the same thing that pulls water up a thin straw or into a cloth. Molten filler is drawn through a brazed joint in the same way, but only if:

ul: the gap is **small and even** (often about 0.05–0.15 mm for silver alloys);
the surfaces are **clean and free of oxide**, so the filler can **wet** them (spread and stick, instead of balling up like water on a greasy plate);
both parts are **at brazing temperature** all over the joint area. Molten filler flows towards the **hottest** part of the joint.

blocks.p: Heated metal oxidises fast, and filler will not wet oxide. **Flux** dissolves the thin oxide that is there, stops new oxide forming while the joint heats, and lets the filler wet the metal. The molten filler then pushes the flux out of the joint ahead of it. A good joint therefore needs clean metal **and** the right flux, put on before heating.

ul: Most fillers do not melt at one temperature. The **solidus** is where the filler starts to melt; the **liquidus** is where it is fully liquid. The brazing temperature is a little above the liquidus.
A filler with a **narrow** melting range (for example 620–655 °C) runs freely into a fine, tight gap.
A filler with a **wide** range (for example 665–755 °C) is sluggish: it is mushy over a wide band, so it can bridge a wider, uneven gap and build a fillet.
If a wide-range filler is heated **slowly**, the part that melts first can run away and leave a lumpy, higher-melting part behind: **liquation**. Heat quickly through the melting range.

head: Advantages
Limits
rows: Lower heat: less distortion, less damage to the metal's properties
Joins unlike metals (copper to steel, steel to brass, carbide to steel)
Thin and thick parts can be joined
Neat joints that often need no finishing
Suits production: many joints at once
Strength depends on a close fit and a large joint area
Joints can be weakened by heat in service above the filler's limit
Toxic fume if the wrong filler or coating is heated

blocks.note: Jamaica's many air-conditioning and refrigeration systems, solar water heaters and copper plumbing jobs mean brazing skills are in steady demand. Refrigerant handling itself is a job for a certified refrigeration technician: the brazer works with them, not in their place.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Safety: fumes, fire, gas and pressure

head: Hazard
Where it comes from
Controls
rows: Old or unlabelled silver brazing alloys; some old fittings
Never use an unlabelled rod: treat it as containing cadmium
Cadmium fume can cause severe lung damage, even death, from one exposure
Brass and brass rods overheated; galvanised steel
Do not overheat brass (white fume is a warning)
Causes **metal fume fever**: shivers, fever, aching muscles a few hours later, like flu
Flux fume and flux on skin
Fluorides and borates in most fluxes
Gloves; wash hands before eating, drinking or smoking
Flux irritates skin and eyes and is harmful if swallowed
Paint, oil and plastic on the parts; chlorinated degreasers near the flame
Keep chlorinated solvents away from flames and hot metal: heat turns their vapour into **phosgene**, a highly toxic gas
Flames, hot parts and dropped filler near wood, rags, insulation, ceilings
Clear or cover anything that burns; heat shields and firebricks
Extinguisher at hand; hot work permit where the site needs one
**Fire watch** after the work for the time the permit or rules set
Air trapped in a closed hollow part (sealed tube, float, tank) expands when heated
Drill a **vent hole** before brazing, or leave the part open
Pipes that still hold refrigerant, gas, fuel or pressure
Never heat a line that is under pressure or holds refrigerant or fuel: a certified technician empties and makes it safe first
Hot parts, the flame, molten filler, bright flux glare
Tinted gas goggles (about shade 3–5), leather gloves, flame-resistant clothing
Mark hot parts HOT; use tongs
Pickle used to clean parts after brazing
When mixing, always add the **acid to the water**, slowly, never water to acid

blocks.p: Use the hierarchy: choose cadmium-free fillers and clean parts (remove the hazard), then **extraction** with the hood close to the joint (an open door or a pedestal fan only spreads the fume round the shop), then PPE such as a respirator if the risk assessment says so. Keep your head out of the plume.

blocks.note: If a member of your team feels shivery and achy, like flu, a few hours after brazing brass or galvanised work, get medical advice for them and check the extraction. Do not send them back to the same job, and do not treat it with home remedies.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Issue only cadmium-free fillers, and remove old or unlabelled stock.
Check extraction, gas equipment, PPE and the fire precautions before anyone lights a torch.
Stop unsafe work at once (no goggles 'for one quick joint', a torch left lit on the bench, a closed part with no vent).
After the work: gas shut down and hoses bled, hot parts marked, flux tubs closed, the area checked for fire for the set time.

head: Gas mixture
Flame temperature (about)
Use in brazing
rows: Hottest, most concentrated flame: heavy steel parts, fast heating, braze welding
Copper tube and light work; gentle, wide heat; simple equipment

head: Flame
How it looks (oxy-acetylene)
Use
rows: Clear, rounded inner cone; no feather
A short white feather round the inner cone
Brazing copper and steel; helps prevent oxide
**Braze welding with brass rod**: the extra oxygen forms a skin on the pool that holds back zinc fume and porosity

blocks.p: For brazing, a **larger, softer flame** that heats the whole joint area evenly is usually better than a small, sharp welding flame that makes a hot spot.

ul: Cylinders upright and chained, in the shade, away from heat and electrical cables. Acetylene cylinders must stand upright: they hold the gas dissolved in acetone.
Never use acetylene above **1 bar** (about 15 psi) on the regulator: above that it can decompose explosively.

Do not draw acetylene too fast (a common rule is no more than about one-seventh of the cylinder contents per hour, or the supplier's figure): acetone is drawn out with the gas. For big heating nozzles, couple two or more cylinders together.
**Flashback arrestors** on both regulators, and non-return valves at the torch. A flashback (flame burning back into the hose) can explode a regulator or cylinder.
Never let oil or grease touch oxygen fittings, and never grease a sticky thread: oxygen makes oil burn violently.
Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothes or the bench, or to 'freshen' air.
Leak-test every connection with leak-detection solution, never with a flame.

flow: Check cylinders, regulators, arrestors, hoses and torch; regulators wound out
Open the cylinder valves slowly; set the working pressures for the nozzle size from the chart
Purge each hose briefly, one at a time, in fresh air
Open the fuel valve a little and light it with a **spark lighter**, never a match or lighter from your pocket
Add oxygen and adjust to the flame you need
To shut down: close the torch valves in the order the supplier and the Centre give; close the cylinder valves; bleed the hoses; wind out the regulators

head: Fault
What it means
Action
rows: Backfire (a sharp pop, flame goes out)
Nozzle too close, overheated or blocked
Shut off, check and clean the nozzle, relight
Flashback (squealing or hissing, flame burning inside the torch)
Flame travelling back up the hose
Shut off oxygen then fuel at the torch at once, close the cylinders; get the equipment checked
Regulator gauge keeps creeping up after the torch is closed
Take the regulator out of use and tag it

head: Method
How it works
Best for
Limits
rows: Repairs, one-off and site work; portable, little set-up
Quality depends on the brazer; slow for large batches
A copper coil carrying high-frequency current heats the joint area only
Runs of identical parts: fast, even and repeatable
A coil must be made to suit each part; costly equipment
Whole assemblies heated in a controlled furnace, often with preformed filler and a protective gas so no flux is needed
Many parts at once; joints hard to reach
Costly; the whole part gets hot
Current passed through the parts between electrodes

head: Filler
Melting range (typical)
Joins
Points to know
rows: About 620–790 °C; higher silver melts lower and flows more freely
Steel, stainless steel, copper, brass, nickel, and unlike metals
Choose one listed for stainless steel when joining stainless
Copper to copper (self-fluxing); copper to brass with flux
The phosphorus cleans copper oxide, so **no flux on copper to copper**
Silver added makes them less brittle and flow better
**Never on steel, stainless or nickel alloys**: brittle phosphides form at the joint
Brass and bronze rods (about 60% copper, 40% zinc, plus silicon or tin)
Braze welding steel, cast iron, galvanised steel, copper
Borax-type flux; slightly oxidising flame; zinc fume
About 575–590 °C, very close to aluminium's own melting point
Special fluxes; tight temperature control; mostly specialist work
Tri-metal strip (silver alloy on both sides of copper)
Carbide tips to steel tool bodies
The copper layer takes up the stress from different expansion

ul: Rod and wire for hand feeding; strip and foil laid in the joint.
**Preforms**: rings, washers or shapes of filler placed on the joint before heating, so every joint gets the same amount. Used in production.
Pastes: filler powder already mixed with flux.

head: Flux
Active range (typical)
Use
rows: Most silver brazing of copper, brass and steel
Large parts that need long heating, and stainless steel, whose tough chromium oxide needs a flux that stays active longer

ul: Use the flux the **filler maker matches** to the filler and the metals.
White flux is also a **temperature guide**: it dries to a white crust, then turns **clear and runs like water** at about 600 °C, just below the brazing temperature of most silver alloys.
Flux that turns **green or black and stops flowing** is burnt out: the joint has been heated too long or too hot.
Flux residue is corrosive. Remove it after brazing, usually with **hot water** and a brush, or as the maker says; left on, it can corrode the joint in service.
Store flux with the lid on, labelled, away from food, as its **safety data sheet** says.

head: Job
Filler
Flux
rows: Yes: brass's zinc oxide is not cleaned by phosphorus
Steel to copper, steel to brass, steel to steel
Cadmium-free silver alloy listed for stainless
Tri-metal or silver alloy listed for carbide

head: Joint
Strength
Use
rows: Strong: the whole circumference is brazed
Good: angled faces give a larger area than a butt
Strip and bar that must stay the same thickness
Weak in thin sheet: the brazed area is only the edge

ul: A common rule: make the **overlap about three times the thickness of the thinner part**. For 1.2 mm sheet to 2.5 mm plate: 3 × 1.2 = **3.6 mm** overlap at least.
Brazed laps are **strong in shear** (load along the joint) but **weak in peel** (a load prising the edge open). Design so the load acts along the joint.
Brazed area of a socket = π × tube diameter × socket depth. A 22 mm tube in a 15 mm deep socket: 3.14 × 22 × 15 ≈ **1 036 mm²**.

head: Clearance
Result
rows: Filler cannot get in; poor fill; flux trapped
Right (often about 0.05–0.15 mm for silver alloys, or the maker's figure)
Strong capillary pull; thin, even, strong filler film
Capillary action fails; voids; a thick, weaker layer of filler; more filler used

blocks.p: The clearance that matters is the one **at brazing temperature**. When two different metals are joined, they expand by different amounts as they heat, and the gap changes.

ul: If the part that expands **more** is on the **inside** (copper pin in a steel ring), the gap **closes** as it heats: set a larger cold gap.
If it is on the **outside** (steel pin in a copper ring), the gap **opens**: set a closer cold fit.

Change in a diametral gap ≈ diameter × difference in expansion × temperature rise. Example: 25 mm, copper inside steel, heated by 700 °C: 25 × (17 − 12) × 700 ÷ 1 000 000 ≈ **0.09 mm** closer. That is most of a 0.1 mm gap.

flow: **Degrease first** with a suitable cleaner or solvent (never a chlorinated solvent near a flame)
Then remove oxide, rust or scale mechanically (emery cloth, fitting brush, abrasive pad, wire brush) or chemically (pickle)
Remove burrs: cut tube with a **tube cutter**, then remove the burr inside and out with a deburring tool
Do not touch cleaned surfaces with bare fingers
Flux and braze **soon** after cleaning, before new oxide and dirt form

blocks.p: Grind or brush rust off a greasy part and you smear the grease into the surface; degreasing first stops that.

ul: Check the clearance with the parts fitted, and that they are square and aligned.
Use a **light jig** that touches the parts at only a few small points: a heavy jig or a big clamp draws heat out of the joint, so the filler will not flow there.
Let gravity hold parts where you can, and allow for expansion.
Protect nearby seals, valve seats, soft solder joints and plastic with a **wet cloth or heat-sink paste**, and keep the flame off them.
Paint stop-off on areas the filler must not run onto, if the procedure says.
Vent any closed hollow part before heating.

flow: Clean, flux both parts thinly and a little beyond the joint area, so no oxide can form where the filler must wet, and fit them together
Heat the **whole joint area** with a moving flame; put more heat into the **heavier, thicker or more conductive** part, so both reach brazing temperature together
Watch the flux: it bubbles, dries, then turns **clear and fluid** (about 600 °C for white flux)
Touch the rod to the joint on the side **away from the flame**; the hot metal, not the flame, should melt it
Let capillary action draw the filler right through the joint, moving the flame to pull it towards the far side
Feed from **one side only**, so the filler pushes the flux out ahead of it
Stop feeding when a small, even fillet shows all round; take the heat away
Hold the parts still until the filler has fully solidified; cool as the procedure says
Wash off the flux with hot water and a brush, or pickle; inspect

head: Sign
What it means
rows: Filler balls up on the surface and will not run in
Joint not hot enough, dirty or oxidised surface, wrong or burnt-out flux, or the rod melted in the flame
Filler runs only at the edge nearest the flame
Heat uneven; the far side is too cool
Flux green or black, not flowing
Overheated or heated too long; flux used up
Filler runs away down the tube
Tube hotter than the fitting; heat the fitting more
Too hot, too long, or too much filler

blocks.note: Never melt the rod in the flame and drip it onto the joint. Molten filler landing on metal that is below brazing temperature cannot wet it: it sits on the surface and the joint is not filled.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Heat the tube near the socket first, then move the flame onto the fitting, which is heavier, so the whole joint comes up together.
Filler is drawn into a socket even upwards; on a vertical joint feed at the top or bottom edge as the heat directs it.
Braze the joints of an assembly in an order that keeps the flame away from finished joints, and protect nearby finished joints with a wet cloth.

Put flux on sparingly, on the outside of the tube end only, not inside the fitting. On refrigeration and air-conditioning lines any flux left inside is carried round the system, where it contaminates the oil and can block valves.

On refrigeration and air-conditioning lines, pass **dry oxygen-free nitrogen** through the pipe at a gentle flow while brazing. Without it, black oxide scale forms inside, breaks off later and blocks filters and valves. Never use oxygen or compressed air for this.

blocks.p: Braze welding fills a groove or builds a fillet with brass (bronze) filler, like a weld, but without melting the parent metal and without capillary flow. Its lower heat makes it useful for:

ul: **Cast iron**, which cracks easily when fusion welded: less heat means less stress. Bevel the crack or joint to a V, clean it well (cast iron needs the surface graphite cleaned off), preheat the casting evenly if the procedure says, and **cool it slowly** (cover it; never quench it).
**Galvanised steel**: less zinc is burned off round the joint than with arc welding, so more of the coating's protection is kept. Use extraction, as zinc fume is still given off.
Steel, copper and unlike metals where a strong fillet is needed.

flow: Prepare the joint like a weld (a V on thick parts) and clean it
Heat to a dull red (well below melting the parent metal) and flux
**Tin** the surface: melt a thin film of filler that wets the joint faces
Build up the groove or fillet in runs on the tinned surface, with a **slightly oxidising** flame
Cool slowly; remove the flux

blocks.p: When several joints on one part are close together, heating the later ones can remelt the first. **Step brazing** uses fillers with different melting points: the **highest-melting** filler for the first joints, then lower-melting fillers for each later joint. Jewellers do the same with 'hard', 'medium' and 'easy' silver solders.

ul: Do not move the parts until the filler is solid all through.
Do not quench joints between unlike metals (such as steel to copper), or carbide tips, in water: they shrink by different amounts and can crack. Quench only where the procedure allows.
Remove all flux: soak in hot water and brush; pickle where the procedure says, then rinse.
Check that the finished joint is cool before handling, and mark hot work HOT.

head: Method
What it shows
How
rows: After cleaning, in good light, perhaps with a magnifier: a smooth, even **fillet** all round; filler visible at the far side of a socket or lap; no gaps, cracks, pinholes, burnt flux, erosion or filler runs; sizes and positions to the drawing
How much of a lap the filler has wetted and filled
Clamp one part of a sample lap joint in a vice and lever and roll the other part back with pliers, then estimate the bonded area
Voids, trapped flux, fill and erosion inside the joint
Saw across a sample joint, file or polish the face smooth, look with a magnifier
Coloured liquid, wait, wipe, apply developer, look for lines
Leaks and weak joints in pipe assemblies
Fill with water, bleed out all air, pump up with a hand test pump to the set pressure with a checked gauge, hold for the set time, check every joint and the gauge
Leaks in refrigeration and air-conditioning lines
Done by the refrigeration technician with dry nitrogen through a regulator, to the equipment maker's pressure; water must never get into these lines

blocks.note: Never pressure test with compressed air or oxygen in the workshop. Compressed gas stores a lot of energy: if a joint fails, pieces fly. A water test that fails just leaks and the pressure drops. Stand clear of any assembly under test and never go above the set pressure.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Record the job number, the joints checked (number them on a sketch), the test, the pressure and hold time, the gauge used, the results, any repairs and re-tests, the date and your name, and sign it. Report pressures in the unit the specification uses: 1 bar = 100 kPa ≈ 14.5 psi.

head: Fault
Likely causes
What to change
rows: Part of the joint not hot enough
Heat the whole joint evenly before feeding
Filler fed from both ends, shutting flux in the middle
Correct flux; clean properly; heat faster and not too hot
Erosion (filler has dissolved the parent metal)
Control the filler, for example with preforms
Different expansion with a tight fit
Stress from a poor joint design
Zinc boiling from overheating; wrong flame
Heat quickly through the melting range

blocks.note: When a joint fails, find the cause before you repair it. Remaking the joint the same way usually gives the same failure.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning, procedures and leading the team

blocks.p: A written brazing procedure makes sure every brazer makes the joint the **same way**, with the same filler, flux, clearance and heat, and gives proof of how the job was done. It includes:

ul: the parent metals and their thickness or size;
the joint type, overlap and clearance;
the filler (type and form) and the flux;
the cleaning method;
the heating method, gas, nozzle and flame;
how the filler is fed, the order of the joints, and any jig, heat sink or nitrogen purge;
cooling and cleaning after brazing;
the inspection and tests, and what counts as a pass;
a number, a date and the name of the person who approved it.

blocks.p: Before production, the procedure is **proved on sample joints**: they are inspected, then peeled or sectioned. If they show voids, trapped flux or erosion, the procedure is changed and tried again. Once proven, the results can be shown to the customer or inspector.

flow: Read the drawing and order: metals, joint types, sizes, number of joints, tests
Write or check the procedure; choose cadmium-free filler and matching flux
Work out materials with an allowance for waste, and book the gas set and extraction
Choose the heating method: torch for one-offs and repairs; induction or furnace for long runs of identical parts
Share out the work: cleaning and fitting, brazing, inspecting
Prove the procedure on sample joints; brief the team on safety
Check joints as they are made; test; record the batch, tests, results and repairs

head: Sum
Example
rows: 45% silver in a 100 g coil: 0.45 × 100 = 45 g
180 joints ÷ 20 good joints an hour = 9 hours

ul: **Preforms** put the same amount of filler on every joint, cut waste and speed up the work.
**Jigs** hold every part in the same place.
**Induction** or **furnace** heating gives the same heat every time, so results do not depend on one brazer's eye.
Check the first joints of a run (first-off) and samples during it.

flow: Watch the trainee braze a joint without stepping in; check the parts, the flux, the flame and the gas set
Name the likely cause (for example: filler balling up because the joint is not hot enough or the rod is melted in the flame)
Correct the cleaning, flux or flame size
Show the right method: even heat, flux turns clear, rod onto the hot joint away from the flame
Let them make sample joints while you watch; peel or section one
Praise good joints and record the coaching
Make it safe: isolate the system; a certified technician recovers any refrigerant and removes the pressure
Look at the joint and around it: is the leak in the joint, beside it, or a crack in the pipe? Is there vibration, rubbing or poor support?
Check the job records: who made it, which filler and procedure, was it tested?
If the joint is cut out, examine the cut faces for voids, poor fill, erosion or cracks
Decide the likely cause and the repair; remake and test
Write the report: date, place, job number, what was found, photos, cause, repair, test results after repair, and what will change; sign and date it

blocks.note: A good report names the joints, the test, the results, the likely cause and the action taken. It is about the facts and the fix, not about blaming a person.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain the difference between soldering, brazing, silver soldering, braze welding and welding.
I can explain capillary action, wetting, flux, solidus, liquidus and liquation.
I can control cadmium, zinc, flux, solvent, fire, bursting and pressure hazards.
I can set up, leak-test, light, adjust and shut down a gas set, and act on backfire, flashback and a creeping regulator.
I can choose torch, induction or furnace heating for a job.
I can choose a filler and flux for copper, brass, steel, stainless steel, cast iron and carbide.
I can design a joint: type, overlap, clearance and loading.
I can work out how expansion changes a gap, and set the cold clearance.
I can clean, fit, jig and protect parts for brazing.
I can braze with even heat, feeding filler at the right time and place.
I can braze weld cast iron and galvanised steel, and plan step brazing.
I can inspect joints and carry out peel, section and pressure tests safely.
I can name brazing faults and their causes, and change the procedure to cure them.
I can write and prove a brazing procedure and work out materials, cost and time.
I can coach a trainee and investigate and report a failed joint.

terms: Braze welding
Laying brazing filler in a groove or fillet like a weld, without capillary flow
Brazing
Joining with a filler that melts above 450 °C but below the parent metals, drawn in by capillary action
Cadmium-free
A filler with no cadmium; the only kind to use
Capillary action
The pull that draws a liquid into a narrow gap
Clearance
The gap between the parts of a brazed joint
Erosion
Filler dissolving the parent metal, from too much heat, time or filler
Fillet
The small, smooth curve of filler at the edge of a good brazed joint
Firebrick
A heat-resistant block that work is laid on for brazing
Flashback arrestor
A safety device on the regulator that stops a flame travelling back into the cylinder
Flux
A chemical that removes and prevents oxide so the filler can wet the metal
Liquation
Part of a wide-range filler melting and running off, leaving a lumpy residue
Liquidus
The temperature at which a filler is fully liquid
Metal fume fever
Flu-like illness from breathing zinc or other metal fume
Peel test
Prising a lap joint open to see how much was wetted
Pickle
A mild acid bath that removes oxide and flux after brazing
Preform
A ring or shape of filler placed on the joint before heating
Silver soldering
Trade name for brazing with silver alloys
Solidus
The temperature at which a filler starts to melt
Step brazing
Using fillers with lower melting points for each later joint, so earlier joints do not remelt
Tinning
Wetting the joint faces with a thin film of filler before building up a braze weld
Vent hole
A hole that lets heated air escape from a closed part
Wetting
Molten filler spreading over and bonding to the clean metal surface

c1.title: Cold-room pipework in Lucea
c1.text: Odane's team is installing the copper pipework for a new cold room at a supermarket in Lucea, Hanover, working with a certified refrigeration technician. The copper-to-copper joints are brazed with a copper-phosphorus filler with 5% silver. Each line also joins a brass service valve. The pipework is new, has never held refrigerant, and will be pressure tested before it is charged.

c2.title: Solar water-heater headers in Christiana
c2.text: A small factory in Christiana, Manchester, makes solar water heaters. Each collector has a 22 mm thick-walled copper header with 10 thin 12 mm copper riser tubes brazed into it, and the factory plans to make 120 collectors a month. At present, brazers feed filler by hand from a rod, and the amount on each joint varies. Some customers have reported green crust and pitting round the joints a few weeks after installation.

c3.title: Repairs to a pump and a railing in Black River
c3.text: Delroy runs a repair shop in Black River, St Elizabeth. A farmer has brought a cracked cast iron pump housing, and a guest house wants a broken joint on its galvanised steel balcony railing repaired. Delroy plans to braze weld both with a brass (bronze) rod and borax-based flux, using an oxy-acetylene set.

c4.title: Trainees' test laps in Brown's Town
c4.text: At a training centre in Brown's Town, St Ann, Level 3 trainees are brazing mild steel to copper lap joints with a cadmium-free silver alloy and white flux, then peel testing them. On one trainee's joint, the peeled lap shows a bare, unwetted patch in the middle with black, burnt flux on it. Another trainee dropped a hot steel-to-copper joint into a bucket of water to cool it, and it cracked. A third keeps heating the rod with the flame and feeding it on the same side as the flame.

c5.title: Brass trophy stands in Half Way Tree
c5.text: A workshop in Half Way Tree, Kingston, makes brass trophy stands with three silver-brazed joints close together. When the third joint is brazed, the first one remelts and moves. The shop stocks a 56% silver alloy (melting range about 620–655 °C) and a 25% silver alloy (about 700–790 °C). Parts are cleaned afterwards in a pickle, which a new worker is about to mix up from concentrated acid.

questions.q: What must be added when the copper-phosphorus filler is used on the copper-to-brass valve joints?
o: Nothing, as copper-phosphorus fillers never need any flux
A flux suited to the filler, as brass is not self-fluxing
A thin steel shim, so that the filler can grip the brass
An extra phosphorus paste to make the filler run thinner
questions.why: The phosphorus cleans copper oxide, so copper-to-copper joints need no flux. Brass contains zinc, whose oxide phosphorus does not remove, so a flux suited to the filler is needed on copper-to-brass joints.

questions.q: Why does the technician want dry nitrogen passed through the pipes while they are brazed?
o: To stop oxide scale forming inside that would later block the system
To cool each joint quickly so that the filler sets before it runs off
To push the molten filler right through the joint from the inside
To test the joints for leaks while the brazing is still going on
questions.why: Hot copper exposed to air inside forms black oxide scale that flakes off later and blocks filters, valves and capillary tubes. A gentle flow of dry, oxygen-free nitrogen keeps air out of the bore.

questions.q: Which flame setting suits brazing these copper joints?
o: Strongly oxidising, to burn the oxide off
Neutral or slightly reducing
Any setting, as long as the flame is small
Slightly oxidising, to hold back zinc fume
questions.why: A neutral or slightly reducing flame heats without adding oxide to the copper. A slightly oxidising flame is for braze welding with brass rod; a small, sharp flame makes hot spots instead of heating the joint evenly.

questions.q: On the copper-to-brass valve joints, why should the flux go thinly on the outside of the tube end only, not into the valve's socket?
o: Flux inside the socket would stop the filler from being drawn in
Brass valves are made with a coat of flux already inside the socket
Flux left inside is carried round the system and contaminates it
Flux on the inside would make the valve's seal set too hard to turn
questions.why: Flux pushed into the bore is left inside the pipework, where it is carried round the system, contaminates the oil and can block valves and filters. A thin coat on the outside of the tube end is drawn into the joint as it is brazed.

questions.q: Why would preformed rings of filler help the factory?
o: They let the brazers use a much smaller flame on each joint
They mean that the joints no longer need to be fluxed at all
Every joint gets the same amount of filler, with less waste
They allow a much wider gap between the riser and the header
questions.why: A preform placed on each joint before heating gives the same filler every time, so the joints are consistent, waste is lower and the work is faster. Flux, flame size and clearance still follow the procedure.

questions.q: Where should a brazer put most of the heat when brazing a thin riser into the thick header?
o: On the thin riser tube, because it is the part the filler must wet
On the filler rod, so that it is fully molten as it meets the joint
On the far side of the header, away from where the riser enters
On the thick header, so both parts reach brazing heat together
questions.why: The thick header takes much longer to heat and conducts heat away. Heating it more, with a little on the riser, brings both to brazing temperature together; heating the thin tube most overheats it while the header stays too cool.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the green crust and pitting round the joints in service?
o: Flux residue left on the joints after brazing
Too little filler fed into each of the joints
The copper riser tubes being too thin for use
The solar heaters being installed in strong sun
questions.why: Brazing flux residue is corrosive and attracts moisture. Left on, it corrodes the copper round the joint. Washing every joint in hot water and brushing it after brazing removes the residue.

questions.q: Why is braze welding a good choice for the cracked cast iron pump housing?
o: The bronze filler is harder and more wear-resistant than the iron
The parent metal is not melted, so there is less heat and stress
It needs no cleaning, because the flux burns off any graphite
It lets the repair be quenched straight away to save time
questions.why: Cast iron is brittle and cracks easily under the heat and shrinkage of fusion welding. Braze welding works well below its melting point, so there is less stress; it still needs careful cleaning and slow cooling.

questions.q: How does braze welding the railing joint differ from a capillary brazed joint?
o: The parent metal is melted together with the filler, just as in welding
It needs a gap of only about 0.05 mm so the filler is drawn in
It uses filler that melts below 450 °C, like a soft solder
The filler fills a groove or builds a fillet, without capillary flow
questions.why: In braze welding the filler is laid in a prepared groove or as a fillet, like a weld, but the parent metal is not melted. Capillary brazing relies on a very close gap to draw the filler in.

questions.q: Why is braze welding often preferred to arc welding for repairing galvanised steel?
o: It gives off no fume, so no extraction is needed
Zinc helps the bronze filler flow into the joint
Galvanised steel cannot be arc welded at all
It burns off less zinc, so more coating is kept
questions.why: Braze welding uses less heat, so less of the zinc coating round the joint is burned away and more corrosion protection remains. Zinc fume is still given off, so extraction is still needed.

questions.q: How should Delroy cool the cast iron housing after the braze weld?
o: Dip it in water at once to set the bronze
Cool it slowly, covered, away from draughts
Blow compressed air over it to cool it evenly
Rest it on the cold concrete floor to draw the heat out
questions.why: Fast or uneven cooling sets up stresses that crack brittle cast iron. Covering the casting and letting it cool slowly in still air keeps the stress low.

questions.q: What most likely caused the bare, unwetted patch with black flux in the middle of the lap?
o: The joint was heated so long that the flux there burnt out
Too much filler was fed into the lap at the start of the joint
The gap at the middle of the lap was far too small for filler
The flux was put on too thickly, so the filler could not reach
questions.why: Black, burnt flux means it was overheated or heated too long and stopped protecting the metal, so oxide formed and the filler could not wet that area. Heat more quickly and evenly, with the right amount of the right flux.

questions.q: Why did the steel-to-copper joint crack when it was dropped into the water?
o: Water reacts with silver alloys and makes them brittle
The water washed the flux out of the joint before the filler set
The two metals shrank by different amounts as it cooled fast
Steel always cracks when it is cooled from a red heat
questions.why: Copper and steel expand and contract by different amounts. Quenching makes them shrink fast and unevenly, which can crack the joint. Let unlike-metal joints cool in still air unless the procedure says otherwise.

questions.q: How should the third trainee be taught to feed the filler?
o: Melt it in the flame first, so it flows straight into the gap
Feed it on the side nearest the flame, where the joint is hottest
Feed it only after the flux has gone black, to show heat
Touch it on the hot joint away from the flame, once flux is clear
questions.why: The hot metal, not the flame, should melt the filler, once the whole joint is at temperature and the flux has turned clear. Filler flows towards the heat, so feeding on the far side draws it right through the joint.

questions.q: How should the workshop braze the three joints so that the first does not remelt?
o: Use the 25% alloy for the early joints and the 56% alloy for the last
Use the 56% alloy for the early joints and the 25% alloy for the last
Braze all three joints with the 56% alloy, using a much smaller flame
Braze all three joints at once with the 25% alloy and extra flux
questions.why: In step brazing, the first joints use the filler with the higher melting range (25% silver, about 700–790 °C) and the last joint the lower-melting one (56%, about 620–655 °C), which can be brazed below 700 °C without remelting the earlier joints.

questions.q: How should the new worker mix the pickle from concentrated acid?
o: Pour the water quickly into the acid so it dilutes at once
Mix it in a closed steel can and shake it well to blend it
Add the acid slowly to the water, with goggles and gloves
Mix it hot, so that it is ready to use at once
questions.why: Adding water to concentrated acid can make it boil and spit violently. Always add the acid slowly to the water, wearing goggles and gloves, in a suitable container.

questions.q: A 30 mm steel plug fits in a copper ring with a 0.05 mm gap when cold. Copper expands about 17 and steel about 12 millionths per °C. Heated by 650 °C, about what is the gap?
o: About 0.38 mm
It closes up completely
About 0.05 mm, unchanged
About 0.15 mm
questions.why: The outer copper ring expands more, so the gap opens by 30 × (17 − 12) × 650 ÷ 1 000 000 ≈ 0.10 mm, giving about 0.15 mm. Using copper's expansion alone gives 0.38 mm; the gap closes only when the higher-expanding metal is inside.

questions.q: What is the highest pressure at which acetylene should be used from the regulator?
o: About 4 bar (60 psi)
About 1 bar (15 psi)
About 10 bar (145 psi)
Whatever the nozzle chart asks
questions.why: Above about 1 bar acetylene can decompose explosively, so regulators and nozzle charts keep it at or below that. Large nozzles needing more gas are supplied from cylinders coupled together, not by raising the pressure.

questions.q: What makes a joining process brazing rather than soft soldering?
o: The filler melts above 450 °C but below the parent metals
The filler contains silver, whatever its melting point is
The parent metals melt into the filler at the joint
The joint is made with a gas torch, not an iron
questions.why: The dividing line is the filler's melting point: above 450 °C is brazing, below it is soldering. Some tin-silver solders melt at about 220 °C and are soft solders; if the parent metal melts, it is welding.

questions.q: A trainee wants to put grease on a sticky oxygen regulator thread. What should you tell him?
o: Use only a little, wiped thin with a clean, dry rag
Never: oil or grease on oxygen fittings can ignite
Use grease only on the cylinder end, never on the hose end
Use it, but open the cylinder valve very slowly
questions.why: Oxygen under pressure makes oil and grease burn violently, even explode. Never lubricate oxygen fittings; a sticky or damaged regulator is taken out of use and repaired by a competent person.
